Subscribe Forecast Discussion High pressure anchored along the Mid-Atlantic coast will send warmer southerly breezes into western North Carolina and Southwest Virginia. Expect picture-perfect weather with unseasonably warm temperatures through Friday. Changes happen rapidly by Friday night as a cold front pushes southward through the area. Over the weekend, the front pulls up stationary to our south as ripples low-pressure travel along it. As a sidebar, some of the moisture and energy associated with the former Hurricane Polo from the eastern Pacific will get infused within this frontal boundary. Showers arrive as soon as Friday night, continuing on Saturday. A cooler wedge will develop on Sunday with additional periods of rain. A second front pushes through Sunday night with clearing, followed by a cool, Canadian high pressure system building-in for the early to middle part of next week. Taken as a whole, October will run slightly warmer and slightly drier than average. The lead graphic shows the expected monthly anomalies for temperature (warmer) and precipitation (drier). The Typical October: The Turn to Fall "Then summer fades and passes and October comes. We'll smell smoke then, and feel an unexpected sharpness, a thrill of nervousness, swift elation, a sense of sadness and departure."— Asheville’s Thomas Wolfe, in “You Can’t Go Home Again” October is the month the season turns. Average highs fall almost ten degrees from September, and average lows fall more than that. The first frost arrives in the mountain region (and maybe the Foothills) most years, and a touch of snow is possible by the end of the month for elevations above 2500’. The chill, the unease (or thrill for some) of colder weather, and the truth that our summer is over—Wolfe captured all that. October is also one of the driest months of the year. Summer thunderstorms are difficult to generate. Rain comes from fronts and from what the tropics send our way. The leaves turn from the high peaks in early October to the Foothills by month’s end.

The Big Picture The cover image for this document shows the ECMWF forecast for precipitation and temperature anomalies in October. We agree with its temperature guidance but favor a slightly wetter month, for reasons given below. The first few days of October will be the warmest of the month by a wide margin. High pressure will hold over the East while the remnants of a Pacific hurricane lift Gulf moisture into the region. The result is a warm, humid, wet start. The heaviest rain will fall over the southern mountains. The High Country, the Foothills and southwest Virginia will get less. A Canadian front will drive through by October 5th, ending the warm spell and bringing drier weather. Cold air will bank against the east side of the Blue Ridge. The Foothills will run cooler than the mountains for a few days under the clouds. The fly in the ointment is a large area of rain to our south. One model brings it north into the region. It is worth watching. The second half of the month is less certain. The models disagree more than usual on where the ridge sits, but none of them shows a major cold outbreak. Temperatures will run near average. With the season falling fast, near average will feel like fall. Rain will run below average in the third week and slightly below in the fourth. Three things concern us about the rain forecast. First, one good rain event can wipe out three dry weeks, as it did in September. Second, El Niño’s moisture from the south becomes more of a factor as October ends. Third, while an Atlantic tropical system is unlikely to reach us, another Pacific storm remnant could, as Hurricane Polo will in the first week. None of these is in the forecast, but all are on the table as a record-breaking El Niño develops. That looming challenge in the Pacific curbed our enthusiasm for a drier or warmer forecast. For reference, the NOAA October forecast as of the date of this publication is similar on temperatures but slightly wetter than our forecast. The Ocean: El Niño Stays on Track El Niño keeps strengthening on schedule. Sea surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region now run more than 2°C above average. The Climate Prediction Center gives better than a 90% chance of a very strong event this fall and winter. There is a strong possibility it will pass 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 as the strongest El Niño on record. No event since records began in 1950 has held the level now forecast for this winter. As a change of pace this month, here is an animation of El Niño’s development over the last four to five weeks. This one has the classic shape. The warmest water sits in the eastern Pacific off South America, not near the Date Line. Buckle up for an El Niño winter in the Southeast: a very active southern jet stream, more storms, and cooler, wetter weather than average. October is early for those effects. Strong El Niño Octobers tend to run warm across the country, with the wet weather held to the Gulf Coast. The Southeast’s turn to a wet pattern usually comes in late October or November. The real impact arrives in winter. We will publish our 2026-27 Fearless Winter Forecast in the third week of October.
